content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Genomic Sequencing Reveals Hidden Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K School Outbreak in Burundi by October 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Genomic Sequencing Reveals Hidden Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K School Outbreak in Burundi Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In January 2026, health authorities in Burundi confronted a familiar and unsettling scenario. A secondary school in Bujumbura reported a sharp increase in respiratory illness among its students, and the immediate suspicion fell on SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. The prospect of a resurgence in a densely populated school setting was a serious concern for the national public health system. Yet when symptomatic students were tested for SARS-CoV-2, the results came back negative, leaving clinicians and epidemiologists with a cluster of unexplained severe acute respiratory infections and no identified cause. That diagnostic dead end is precisely where the investigation described in a study published in BMC Infectious Diseases begins. A team led by Néhémie Nzoyikorera of the National Reference Laboratory at the National Public Health Institute in Burundi, working with colleagues at Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam and partners across East Africa, Morocco, and Germany, applied targeted viral enrichment sequencing to nasopharyngeal samples collected from symptomatic students. The approach was designed to cast a wide net: rather than testing for one pathogen at a time, the method enriches and sequences viral genetic material present in a sample, allowing researchers to identify whatever viruses are there, known or unknown. The technical foundation of the investigation rests on the Illumina Viral Surveillance Panel version 2, run on the compact iSeq 100 sequencing platform. Eight samples from SARS-CoV-2-negative students were processed through this targeted enrichment workflow. The panel uses probes designed to capture viral genomes across a broad range of respiratory and other viruses, concentrating scarce viral nucleic acid against a background of human DNA and other genetic noise. After sequencing, the reads were quality-checked, screened for viral identification, and then assembled into genome sequences where coverage permitted. The results were decisive. Influenza A virus was detected in seven of the eight samples analyzed, and four of those samples yielded near-complete influenza A genomes of sufficient quality for detailed genomic characterization. When the researchers assigned clades to the reconstructed genomes, every characterized virus fell into the same category: Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K. This was the first genomic detection and characterization of that subclade in Burundi, a finding that carries significance well beyond the school gates because H3N2 subclade K has been drawing attention internationally as an emerging variant of the seasonal influenza virus. Influenza A(H3N2) is one of the seasonal influenza A subtypes that circulates in human populations and is notorious for its capacity to evolve rapidly. The hemagglutinin protein, the HA of H3N2, is the primary target of protective antibodies, and mutations accumulating in the HA gene allow the virus to escape immunity built up through previous infections and vaccination. Clade and subclade designations, such as subclade K, are assigned on the basis of characteristic amino acid signatures in HA, and they help global surveillance laboratories track which genetic variants are spreading, which are vaccine-matched, and which signal a need for updated vaccine composition. Phylogenetic analysis of the Burundian sequences added a layer of complexity to the outbreak picture. The sequences did not form a single tight cluster. Instead, they split into two distinct groups on the phylogenetic tree, suggesting that at least two separate viral lineages of H3N2 subclade K were circulating during the outbreak. This observation matters for outbreak interpretation. A single introduction followed by onward transmission would typically produce a compact cluster of closely related genomes, whereas the presence of divergent lineages points to multiple introductions or to undetected circulation in the community before the school cluster was recognized. Genomic analysis was therefore able to reveal structure in the outbreak that routine testing alone could not. The researchers also examined the neuraminidase sequences for markers associated with resistance to neuraminidase inhibitors, the class of antiviral drugs that includes oseltamivir. No resistance-associated markers were detected, an important clinical finding because it indicates that antiviral treatment would be expected to remain effective against the circulating viruses if severe cases required it. The absence of resistance markers also provides reassurance for national treatment guidelines and for any future response to H3N2 subclade K in the region. To ensure the findings contributed to the global picture, the influenza genome sequences were shared through GISAID, the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data, which serves as the central repository for influenza sequence data used by the World Health Organization and surveillance laboratories worldwide. Sharing genomes from Burundi addresses a longstanding gap in global influenza surveillance, which has historically been dominated by data from high-income countries in temperate regions. Sequences from African settings, particularly from outbreaks identified through unexplained severe acute respiratory infection surveillance, help clarify how subclade K and other variants move between regions and how they evolve in different population contexts. The study also underscores the value of severe acute respiratory infection surveillance as a pillar of emerging disease preparedness. The samples in this investigation had been collected initially for SARI surveillance, and the national ethics framework, including approval by the National Ethics Committee of Burundi with a consent waiver, allowed their use for pathogen identification. When the initial hypothesis of a COVID-19 resurgence collapsed, the surveillance infrastructure and the stored samples provided the raw material for a rapid pivot to unbiased pathogen detection. The Burundi Public Health Emergency Operation Center supported the epidemiological investigations, and reagents were provided through the East African Community Secretariat’s Mobile Lab Project, illustrating how regional cooperation underpins laboratory response capacity. The broader lesson from the Bujumbura school outbreak is that targeted viral enrichment sequencing is a practical tool for investigating acute respiratory outbreaks when the cause is unknown, particularly when initial testing is negative and routine testing for other respiratory viruses is limited. In settings where multiplex PCR panels are expensive or unavailable, a single sequencing run can identify the pathogen, characterize its genome, assign its clade, screen for resistance markers, and place it in a global phylogenetic context. The first genomic characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K in Burundi demonstrates that genomic surveillance capacity, strengthened through projects such as GREAT-LIFE at the national public health institute, can deliver actionable findings from a modest number of samples, and that the identification of distinct viral lineages within a single school outbreak highlights the value of genomic approaches to complement routine laboratory testing and support respiratory pathogen surveillance in Burundi and across the region. Health Flu season started earlier than expected — what to know about the brand new vaccine By Allie Yang Published Oct. 14, 2026, 3:16 p.m. ET 1616 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Now is around the time when flu season usually starts to pick up — except this year, cases have been rising since late summer. Some data shows current flu activity is similar to when flu activity peaks at the end of the year. But it’s still too early to tell whether this year’s flu will be particularly severe. For now, experts are warning people take precautions: Avoid people who are sick, wash your hands — and get vaccinated. This year, there’s a brand new shot that takes a totally different approach to flu prevention, and early data shows it’s more effective than the traditional shot. But it’s not for everyone. Here’s what to know. Some data shows flu activity is similar to what’s normally seen at the end of the year, when flu season peaks. alfa27 – stock.adobe.com Rising flu cases October is the typical start of the flu season. But this year, cases started rising as early as late August. Based on wastewater data, flu activity reached levels this month usually not seen until December or January — when flu season historically peaks. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said. That said, a vast majority of the country remains in “minimal” range of flu cases. “Every influenza season is different — some begin earlier than usual, others later,” the CDC said. Despite an early start to flu season, 2026’s flu trends remain “within expected seasonal variation.” And while the flu generally starts picking up in southern states, this year, it appeared first in the West: California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska. Some experts say these changes might point to an evolving flu virus. ‘Stick’ season An earlier flu season means considering getting an earlier flu shot, experts say. And this year, there’s a brand new one on the market. In August, the FDA approved mFLUSIVA, the first mRNA flu vaccine for adults aged 50 and older. Everyone ages 6 months and up should get an annual flu vaccine, the CDC says. AntonioDiaz – stock.adobe.com Unlike traditional flu vaccines, it does not contain a weakened or inactive flu virus. Instead, it works by giving instructions via mRNA to your immune cells on how to kill the flu virus on its own. This is the same technology used in the COVID-19 vaccines. “There is some evidence that suggests mFlusiva may offer somewhat better protection against the flu than traditional flu vaccines,” Dr. Rebecca Choudhury, an infectious disease doctor at Mount Sinai, said. In adults 50 and older, the mRNA vaccine had a 27% lower rate of flu infection compared to traditional vaccines. Adverse reactions to the new vaccine were very rare, and happened at similar rates to side effects to the traditional flu vaccine. Choudhury says adults aged 50 to 64 have the clearest reason to consider it, and especially those with chronic health conditions that raise the risk of a severe case of flu. That said, it’s a very new drug that may not be available at every doctor’s office or pharmacy — and Choudhury says it’s better to get the traditional shot rather than go without. Everyone six months and older should get an annual flu shot, the CDC says. This year’s traditional flu vaccines target three flu viruses — H1N1 and H3N2 (both subtypes of the more common influenza A) and influenza B. 16 What do you think? Post a comment. According to CDC data, over 75% of positive flu tests are H1N1 for the last month. It’s been circulating since it emerged as “swine flu” in 2009 and has become a regular part of flu season, joining a number of other influenza A and B strains that come back every year. This year’s vaccine was adjusted to protect against a H3N2 mutation called “subclade K” that spread widely last year. This type of flu causes typical flu symptoms like fever and cough to come on more abruptly. SPONSORED STORIES

content: This Year’s Flu Season Started Early—And the Typical Vaccine Deadline May Be Too Late While you normally only hear about a surge of flu cases during the deep winter months, it's still early fall and the U.S. is already seeing flu at higher-than-usual rates. A recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that seasonal flu activity is "increasing" in many parts of the country, though it is still generally low. Based on the latest data, 3.6% of Americans tested for a respiratory issue were also positive for the flu. "Flu season is happening much earlier than usual," says Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York. "The beginning of influenza season is always unpredictable—this is another example." What's driving this increase in cases and, more importantly, how can you stay healthy? Here's what you need to know. Meet the experts: Asefeh Faraz Covelli, PhD, APRN, researcher and associate professor at The George Washington University School of Nursing and Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York Where are flu cases increasing? The flu doesn't hit the country at the same level, at the same time. Right now, for example, the CDC points out that the highest flu activity is happening on the West Coast. California's test positivity rate for influenza currently sits at 8.8 percent, based on state data, while Alaska's public health department noted that flu cases started to "increase noticeably" in mid-August. "There isn't one clear explanation for why it's happening earlier this year," says Asefeh Faraz Covelli, PhD, APRN, researcher and associate professor at The George Washington University School of Nursing. "We need to keep watching the data to understand whether this early rise will translate into an earlier or more severe flu season overall." The earlier-than-usual season is largely driven by an H1N1 variant of the flu, with a D.3.1.1 HA subclade. That may be more immune-evasive than other strains, leading to the rise in early infections, Dr. Russo says. But Covelli includes this important caveat: "An earlier start doesn't necessarily mean the flu is stronger." Flu viruses change every year, and some of those changes may make it easier for the virus to spread in people who have some level of immunity already. "Researchers are watching the strains circulating this year, but it's too early to know whether these changes will make this flu season more severe," she says. Flu symptoms to look out for If you're worried you have the flu, keep the following in mind. Flu symptoms don't really change from year to year, and these are the biggest ones to be aware of, per the CDC: - Fever - Cough - Sore throat - Runny or stuffy nose - Muscle or body aches - Headaches - Fatigue When to get vaccinated Public health agencies usually recommend getting vaccinated by Halloween. But given the season's early start, healthcare providers say you're fine to get the vaccine now. "If you haven't gotten your flu shot yet, I'd get it now rather than wait," Covelli says. "September and October are generally the best time to get vaccinated, and it takes about two weeks for your body to build up protection." Getting vaccinated now can help to protect you throughout the season, she says. Also, while it's easy to assume an early start to flu season means it might also end sooner, that's not guaranteed. "Sometimes we have two waves due to influenza A and then influenza B," Dr. Russo says. "We will have to see." You Might Also Like
